label: lf-standards-us
topic: US fire-test requirements for interior wall/ceiling coatings and intumescent coatings, from open sources only
summary: Partly established in about 7 minutes. CONFIRMED-OPEN-SOURCE from pages I opened: the IBC 2021 Chapter 8 text (UpCodes viewer, Colorado adoption) gives the ASTM E84 / UL 723 classes (A 0-25, B 26-75, C 76-200 flame spread; smoke-developed 0-450 for all three) and the five NFPA 286 room-corner acceptance criteria (800 kW peak heat release, 1,000 m2 total smoke, no flashover, no flame to ceiling during the 40 kW exposure, no spread to the sample edge). eCFR 24 CFR 3280.203 (manufactured homes) names ASTM E84-01 (2001) and sets flame spread at most 200 for walls and 75 for ceilings. eCFR 29 CFR 1910.35 names NFPA 101 2009 and IFC 2009. UNCONFIRMED: the ASTM E119 / UL 263 steel temperature limits for intumescent coatings (1000 F average / 1200 F single point for columns) appeared only in search-result snippets, which also conflicted on the beam limits. No E1354 cone calorimeter pass criterion was found; search snippets suggest it is a measurement method with limits set by the adopting code, also unconfirmed. Current edition years of ASTM E84, NFPA 286, E119 and E1354 were not found in any open source I opened; the only edition year confirmed for E84 is the 2001 one frozen into the HUD rule. The IBC 2024 text was not reachable (ICC viewer 403, UpCodes 404), so the IBC numbers are confirmed for the 2021 edition only. No files were written.

lay_summary: In the US, paint or coating on indoor walls and ceilings is graded by a tunnel test that measures how fast flame travels along it and how much smoke it makes.
The best grade, Class A, means a flame-spread score of 0 to 25; Class B is 26 to 75 and Class C is 76 to 200, and all three must keep the smoke score at 450 or less.

Another route is a room-corner test, where a burner is lit in the corner of a test room: the fire must stay under 800 kilowatts, the smoke under 1,000 square metres, and the room must not burst into full flame.
I confirmed these numbers from the 2021 building code text and from federal rules, but could not open the newest 2024 code.
The numbers for puffy fire-protective paint on steel and for the small cone-heater test are not confirmed, because I only saw them in search snippets.

glossary.ASTM E84 / UL 723: The tunnel test: a strip of material is burned in a long tunnel to score flame spread and smoke.
glossary.Flame spread index: A score for how fast flame travels along a surface; lower is safer.
glossary.Smoke-developed index: A score for how much smoke the material gives off in the tunnel test; lower is safer.
glossary.Class A / B / C: Building-code grades for interior finishes based on the tunnel test scores; A is the best.
glossary.NFPA 286: A room-corner fire test where a burner is lit in the corner of a room lined with the material.
glossary.Flashover: The moment a room fire suddenly ignites everything in the room at once.
glossary.Heat release rate (kW): How much heat a fire gives off each second, in kilowatts.
glossary.Total smoke released (m2): A measure of how much smoke the test produced, expressed as an area of light blocked.
glossary.ASTM E119 / UL 263: A furnace test that measures how many hours a wall, floor, beam or column survives a standard fire.
glossary.ASTM E1354 (cone calorimeter): A small bench test where a cone-shaped heater burns a sample to measure heat output.
glossary.ASTM E1740: A test for wall and ceiling coverings that uses the cone calorimeter.
glossary.Intumescent coating: A paint that swells into a thick insulating foam when heated, protecting what is underneath.
glossary.Fire-retardant coating: A coating that slows the spread of flame over a surface.
glossary.IBC: International Building Code, the model building code most US states adopt.
glossary.IFC: International Fire Code, the companion model fire code.
glossary.NFPA 101: The Life Safety Code published by the National Fire Protection Association.
glossary.eCFR: The free online version of US federal regulations.
glossary.Edition year: The year a particular version of a standard or code was published.
glossary.Interior finish: The exposed surface material on indoor walls and ceilings.
glossary.CONFIRMED-OPEN-SOURCE / UNCONFIRMED: Whether I read the number on a freely available page I opened, or not.
